The examples are obstructions to the stated local proof scheme, not counterexamples to Problem 644. $\square$

### 7.67 A complete finite catalogue of bad seven-row supports [C]

The relevant Boolean-function classification is known: Testa, Haaswijk, Soeken and De Micheli, *The Complexity of Self-Dual Monotone 7-Input Functions* (IWLS 2019), report 1422564 labelled functions in 716 permutation classes and supply representatives. Primary sources: [paper](https://si2.epfl.ch/demichel/publications/archive/2019/IWLS_ET.pdf), [authors' data](https://github.com/eletesta/7input_classification). The application here uses their truth-table filenames, not their circuit-complexity claims. The counts and the completeness of the representatives have been independently checked below.

**Lemma 7.65.** Up to permutations of the seven row labels, every bad seven-tuple of nonempty sets has its occupied Venn cells contained in one of 715 explicitly listed downward-closed supports with no covering pair. Every such support yields bad tuples whenever its prescribed positive row sizes can be realized. For intersecting tuples, 604 supports suffice; all their maximal cells have size at most four.

*Support reduction.* Close the occupied cells downwards. No covering pair is introduced: a covering pair of smaller cells would already give a covering pair of their original parents. Extend this downward-closed family $D$ to an inclusion-maximal one with no covering pair. For each $S\subseteq[7]$, at most one of $S,[7]\setminus S$ belongs to $D$. If neither belongs, adding $S$ and its subsets is safe: an existing $T$ with $S\cup T=[7]$ would contain the complement of $S$, which would already belong to $D$. This contradicts maximality. Thus exactly one of each complementary pair belongs to $D$.

The indicator $f(S)=1$ for $S\notin D$ is therefore monotone and self-dual: $f(S)+f([7]\setminus S)=1$. Conversely, every monotone self-dual function gives such a maximal downward support. A function with a winning singleton is a projection, since monotonicity and self-duality then force $f(S)=1$ exactly when that singleton is in $S$. Its losing cells omit one row altogether, so it cannot contain the support of seven nonempty sets. The projection class is the one discarded from the 716 classes.

For an intersecting bad tuple, a point cannot lie in five or more rows: the at most two omitted edges can be met by one additional point. Let $F$ consist of the complements of its occupied four-cells. These are pairwise intersecting triples, and no occupied three-cell belongs to $F$. Hence its support is contained in
$$D_F=\{[7]\setminus T:T\in F\}\ \cup\ \bigl(\tbinom{[7]}3\setminus F\bigr)\ \cup\ \tbinom{[7]}{\le2}.$$
This family is downward closed and has no covering pair. To check downward closure at a four-cell, a three-subset of $[7]\setminus T$ is disjoint from $T$, so cannot belong to the intersecting family $F$. Self-duality follows directly by pairing triples with their four-element complements and pairing smaller sets with larger ones. Thus the extension may be chosen with no cell larger than four.

*Independent exact count and completeness certificate.* A nonprojection monotone self-dual function has no winning singleton and is uniquely determined by its winning pairs $E$ and winning triples $F$. The conditions are exactly:

1. $E$ is pairwise intersecting;
2. $F$ contains every triple containing a member of $E$;
3. every member of $F$ meets every member of $E$, and $F$ is pairwise intersecting.

Necessity follows because two disjoint winning sets would violate monotonicity and self-duality. For sufficiency declare the four-, five-, six- and seven-set values by self-duality. Monotonicity from size two to three is condition 2, and from size three to four follows from intersection of the two triples. If a winning four-set were contained in a losing five-set, the complementary winning pair of that five-set would be contained in the complementary triple of the four-set, forcing that triple to be winning by condition 2, a contradiction. The other adjacent ranks are immediate. This proves sufficiency and uniqueness.

The independent checker enumerates the 456 intersecting families of pairs on seven points, including the empty family. For each, the forced triples are included, and the remaining eligible triples are those meeting every winning pair. A memoized include/exclude clique recurrence counts the pairwise-intersecting choices among them. The total is 1422557 nonprojection functions; adding the seven labelled projections gives 1422564. When $E$ is empty the count is 1278686.

The authors' repository lists 715 nonprojection hexadecimal truth tables. The checker verifies monotonicity and self-duality of every table directly on all 128 inputs. It constructs all 5040 variable permutations, checks that the 715 orbits are disjoint, and that their sizes sum to the independently derived 1422557. These are valid distinct functions in a space of exactly that size, proving exhaustive coverage. Exactly 604 orbits have no winning pair, and their orbit sizes sum to 1278686. Among these, 603 have maximal losing cells of size four and one has maximal cells of size three; the other 111 usable orbits have maximal cells of size five.

The checker also reconstructs each support's maximal cells and verifies directly that no two cover all seven labels and that every losing cell lies below a listed maximal cell. This supplies the explicit catalogue required in the statement. $\square$

Replay is `p644_support_catalog_check.py`, using the saved public registry `external_716_registry.json`. The immutable source tree is `f8df07f4f30d8f9b61eb7befe4d4585b18fb7b75`; the downloaded registry's SHA-256 is `9baf0e585a337149ce296b777aeafaac0eaf751a5a2bec0b09115fa186eef74b`. The self-contained output is `logs/astra_full_support_catalog.json`. Independently, `p644_bad_support_catalog.py` generated all 1278686 intersecting triple families and their 604 orbits directly, agreeing with the appropriate part of the published classification.

This gives a complete replacement for an ad hoc bad-support menu. For fixed component assignments of seven types, use a nonnegative mass variable for each catalogue parent cell in each part, require the parent loads to dominate the prescribed row loads, and impose the part capacities. Row trimming then gives actual bad cells. Conversely, any bad tuple is feasible in one such catalogue LP, after relabelling. This statement uses all 715 supports for general families, or the 604-support subcatalogue for intersecting families. It does not assert that an arbitrary high-transversal family contains those realizations; obtaining that implication is still the unresolved part of Problem 644.

### 7.68 A complete, exactly certifying two-box decision procedure

**Proposition 7.66.** For two rational sliced-box components over any fixed number of parts, existence of a continuous bad seven-tuple is equivalent to feasibility of one of 54214 explicit rational linear programs. A feasible solution supplies an explicit rational bad tuple. Infeasibility of every program has a finite rational Farkas certificate. The number 54214 counts the row-component assignments modulo automorphisms of each of the 715 supports; it does not depend on the number of parts.

*Proof.* Fix a catalogue support with maximal cells $C_1,\ldots,C_q$, a component assignment $\epsilon_j\in\{0,1\}$ for the seven rows, and part capacities $x_i$. Let $y_{it}\ge0$ be masses assigned to parent cell $C_t$ in part $i$. Let $a_{ij}$ be the chosen size of row $j$ in part $i$. The constraints are
$$\sum_t y_{it}\le x_i,\qquad
\ell_{\epsilon_j i}\le a_{ij}\le u_{\epsilon_j i},\qquad
\sum_i a_{ij}=r,\qquad
a_{ij}\le\sum_{t:j\in C_t}y_{it}.$$
If feasible, partition the mass into the parent cells and trim membership in each row until its part size is $a_{ij}$. Trimming a row changes no other row's size and only produces subsets of parent cells, so no covering pair is introduced. Conversely, place each occupied cell of a bad tuple below a catalogue parent containing it and aggregate its mass there. This satisfies the displayed inequalities. Lemma 7.65 proves that some catalogue support contains every possible bad tuple, after relabelling. Automorphisms of that support preserve feasibility, so one component assignment per orbit suffices. Direct enumeration of all seven-row permutations and all 128 assignments gives 54214 orbits in total.

After substituting $a_{ij}=\ell_{\epsilon_j i}+w_{ij}$, all variables are nonnegative and the system has the form $Av\le b$ with an integer matrix $A$. A rational feasible vector is an exact positive certificate. An infeasibility certificate is a rational vector $z\le0$ such that $A^Tz\le0$ and $b^Tz>0$: any feasible $v\ge0$ would imply $0\ge z^TAv\ge z^Tb>0$. Rational linear programming duality supplies such a vector for every infeasible rational system. A bad tuple of fewer than seven edges can be padded by repeating an edge, so this also decides property $(7,2)$ with the at-most-seven convention. This proves the decision reduction and its certificate claims. $\square$

The implementation `p644_support_lp.py` uses numerical phase-I LPs only for discovery. Every result is checked with rational arithmetic before acceptance; failed reconstruction means UNKNOWN. It reuses a Farkas vector only after checking that its strict contradiction remains valid for the new right-hand side. `p644_support_lp_check.py` independently reconstructs every matrix, the complete component-orbit list, and the primal or dual inequalities using only the standard library. Positive certificates also contain explicitly trimmed Venn cells, whose row sizes, box bounds, capacities and absence of a covering pair are checked directly.

**Regression facts [C].** For capacities $(1,1)$ and the two fixed types $(249/1000,751/1000)$ and $(701/1000,299/1000)$, all 54214 programs are infeasible. The certificate uses 4474 exact Farkas vectors; 49740 further assignments reuse one of them. Independent full replay passes. This supplies a second, complete-support verification of the previously known pocket example, whose continuous transversal coefficient is $137/250=0.548$. The same implementation produces and independently checks explicit bad tuples for: the two pure types on capacities $(7/5,7/5)$; the three-part example of Proposition 7.58; and the symmetric quarter/three-quarter two-type family. Data: `logs/astra_support_exact_{pocket,pure,line,quarter}.json`. These checks introduce no new general upper bound.

### 7.69 Exact two-request finishing regions for a candidate-pair graph

**Lemma 7.67.** Let $G$ be a finite simple graph whose vertices stand for disjoint cells of nonnegative masses $m_v$. Its edges represent complete products of candidate piercing pairs. For subsets $A,B\subseteq V(G)$ with no graph edge joining a vertex in $A$ to a vertex in $B$, write
$$C=V(G)\setminus(A\cup B),\quad A_0=A\setminus B,\quad B_0=B\setminus A,$$
and $m(S)=\sum_{v\in S}m_v$. First discard zero-mass vertices, then omit vertices that are isolated in the remaining graph. On this reduced graph the minimum possible maximum mass of two sets covering every candidate pair is
$$\min_{(A,B)}\max\left\{m(C)+m(A_0),\ m(C)+m(B_0),\ \frac{m(V(G))+m(C)}2\right\}.$$
It suffices to minimize over inclusion-maximal anticomplete pairs $(A,B)$, allowing $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$ and identifying the two orders.

*Proof.* Label each point by the nonempty subset of the two requests containing it. Every point in a nonisolated positive-mass cell needs a nonempty label: it is an endpoint of a candidate pair. Labels at opposite ends of every graph edge must intersect. Within a cell, whenever both a label and a strictly larger label occur, replace the larger by the smaller; this preserves all label intersections with other cells and cannot increase either request. Thus the possible minimal label families in a cell are exactly $\{1\}$, $\{2\}$, $\{12\}$, and $\{1,2\}$.

Let $A$ contain cells allowed label 1 and $B$ those allowed label 2. Cross-intersection of labels says exactly that $(A,B)$ is anticomplete. Cells in $C$ belong to both requests; those in $A_0$ and $B_0$ belong to their specified request; cells in $A\cap B$ can be split arbitrarily between requests. With $a=m(C)+m(A_0)$, $b=m(C)+m(B_0)$ and flexible mass $s=m(A\cap B)$, the optimal maximum load is $\max(a,b,(a+b+s)/2)$, the displayed expression. Conversely, every such assignment gives a valid pair cover. Enlarging an anticomplete pair only allows more labels in its cells and cannot increase the optimum; therefore maximal pairs suffice. $\square$

For completeness, put $N(S)=\{v:\text{no edge joins }v\text{ to any }s\in S\}$. A maximal pair satisfies $B=N(A)$ and $A=N(B)$. Enumerating subsets $A$ and retaining those with $A=N(N(A))$ therefore enumerates all finishing regions exactly. This is implemented in `p644_two_finish_adaptive.py`. It permits a new avoidance request, observes its response, and then chooses a region for the final two requests. `p644_adaptive_request_cegis.py` additionally synthesizes partially filled first requests using exact rational adversarial responses. Solver outcomes from these discovery programs are not asserted as universal lemmas until separately checked. This framework enlarges the tested adaptive strategy class; it still chooses the last two requests simultaneously.

**Boundary correction.** The first discovery version omitted the positive-neighbor test and could overcharge a cell joined only to zero-mass cells. For a single graph edge of masses $(1,0)$, its old expression returned $1/2$ although there are no actual pairs and the correct cost is zero. Those first adaptive-search outputs are invalid as obstruction certificates. The corrected version sets a cell's effective mass to zero when all its neighbors have zero mass, and stores outputs in distinct `_v2` directories. The complete-support LP certificates of Section 7.68 do not use this pair-cover formula and are unaffected.

The independent `p644_pair_cover_check.py` compares the corrected formula against exhaustive minimal-label assignments for every simple graph on four labelled vertices and every zero/one mass vector: all 1024 cases pass, including the zero-neighbor regression.

### 7.71 A complete 42-function criterion for two fixed types [C]

**Theorem 7.69.** There is an explicit list of 42 functions $M_1,\ldots,M_{42}$, each the maximum of finitely many nonnegative rational linear forms in two variables, with the following property. Let $a,b\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^p$ be two admissible types of the same positive rank, on parts of capacities $x_i$. The type-closed family with exactly those two types admits a continuous bad seven-tuple if and only if
$$\text{for some }t\in\{1,\ldots,42\},\qquad M_t(a_i,b_i)\le x_i\quad\text{for every part }i.$$
The 42 functions are pairwise incomparable under pointwise order on the nonnegative quadrant. Their coefficients and explicit support/row-colouring witnesses are listed in `logs/astra_support_capacity_minimal.json`. The criterion applies to arbitrary capacities and any number of parts; it does not assume intersectingness. This is a complete decision criterion for two fixed types, not a proof of the general $3/4$ bound.

*Reduction to per-part capacity polygons.* For a maximal support $\mathcal D$ with parent cells $C$, and a colouring $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^7$, give each row load $s$ or $t$ according to its colour. The minimum total parent mass realizing these loads is the covering LP
$$\min\left\{\sum_C y_C:y_C\ge0,\ \sum_{C:j\in C}y_C\ge z_j\ (j\in[7])\right\},$$
where $z_j=s$ or $t$. Every row occurs in a parent cell, so the primal is feasible and its dual polytope
$$P_{\mathcal D}=\left\{w\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^7:\sum_{j\in C}w_j\le1\text{ for every parent }C\right\}$$
is bounded. Project this dual onto
$$u=\sum_{\epsilon_j=0}w_j,\qquad v=\sum_{\epsilon_j=1}w_j.$$
The resulting rational polygon is downward closed in the nonnegative quadrant. Its support function is $M(s,t)=\max(us+vt)$ over its upper vertices, by LP duality. As in Proposition 7.66, parent masses can be trimmed independently in each row. Thus the same support and colouring realize the two types over all parts exactly when $M(a_i,b_i)\le x_i$ for all $i$.

There are 54214 support/colour cases. The exact projections give 11865 distinct functions. If one function is pointwise at most another, its fixed support and colouring provide a realization whenever the other does, simultaneously in every part. Pointwise dominance therefore leaves the existence criterion unchanged. The exact reduction retains 42 functions, each present in the original catalogue; every original function is dominated by a retained one, and no two retained functions dominate one another. Completeness of the support catalogue now proves both directions of the theorem. $\square$

*Independent certificates.* `p644_support_capacity.py` discovers each projected polygon using LP support queries. `p644_support_capacity_check.py` independently verifies 375446 rational primal/dual pairs: all cover inequalities, all dual parent inequalities, equality of objective values, each proposed vertex and every upper polygon facet. It reconstructs the complete component-assignment orbits again and checks that the distinct functions match the dominance file, including the 42 retained construction witnesses. This verifies all 54214 cases without trusting numerical statuses.

`p644_capacity_dominance_check.py` uses a second characterization of dominance. Normalize $(s,t)$ to $(q,1-q)$, $0\le q\le1$. Between consecutive crossings of the upper function's defining lines, it is linear. The difference between the lower support function and that line is convex, so nonpositivity at both interval endpoints implies nonpositivity throughout. Exact evaluation at all such crossings and at 0 and 1 independently verifies the 11865 claimed dominations and pairwise incomparability of the 42 survivors.

The full JSON certificates occupy about 258 MB uncompressed and 10.84 MB in the lossless `capacity_data.zip` bundle. The standard-library checker reads that archive directly; no numerical solver is needed for replay. Rational feasible constructions scale to suitable integer multiples, as in the earlier structured theorems. No stronger rounding statement is asserted.

### 7.72 A tetrahedral construction extracted from the catalogue

**Lemma 7.70.** Partition the seven row labels into $A$ of size four and $B$ of size three. Give every $A$-row load $s\ge0$ and every $B$-row load $t\ge0$ in a part. There is a fixed bad support whose exact minimum required mass is
$$M_{K_4}(s,t)=\max\left\{\frac23s+t,\ \frac43s+\frac12t\right\}.$$
Consequently two admissible types $a,b$ have a bad seven-tuple, four rows of type $a$ and three of type $b$, whenever $M_{K_4}(a_i,b_i)\le x_i$ in every part.

*Proof.* Identify the three elements of $B$ with the three perfect matchings of the complete graph on $A$. The parent cells are: the four triples $A\setminus\{a\}$; the triple $B$; and the six four-sets
$$e\cup(B\setminus\{b\}),\qquad e\text{ an edge in the matching indexed by }b.$$
No two parent cells cover all seven labels. Two four-cells from the same matching omit the same element of $B$. Two from different matchings have intersecting $A$-edges, so together cover at most three elements of $A$. All other pairs either cover at most three elements of $A$, or at most two elements of $B$. Downward closure is therefore a bad support.

Three explicit mass assignments realize the load pairs $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(3,4)$. For $(1,0)$, put mass $1/3$ on each of the four $A$-triples; the total is $4/3$. For $(0,1)$ put mass one on $B$. For $(3,4)$ put mass one on each of the six four-cells; each $A$-row occurs in one edge of each matching, and each $B$-row in four four-cells, so the loads and total mass six are correct.

If $s\le3t/4$, combine $(s/3)$ times the $(3,4)$ assignment with $(t-4s/3)$ times the $(0,1)$ assignment. The total mass is $2s/3+t$. If $s\ge3t/4$, combine $(t/4)$ times the $(3,4)$ assignment with $(s-3t/4)$ times the $(1,0)$ assignment. Its mass is $4s/3+t/2$. Both combinations use nonnegative masses and give exactly the desired row loads.

For optimality, assign dual weight $1/6$ to each $A$-row and $1/3$ to each $B$-row. Every parent cell has weight at most one, giving the lower bound $2s/3+t$. Swapping these two weights gives the other lower bound $4s/3+t/2$. The constructions attain their maximum, proving the formula. Applying this construction independently in each part proves the final assertion. $\square$

This support has eleven maximal cells and is different from the seven-parent Fano support. The new coupling inequalities are $2a_i+3b_i\le3x_i$ and $8a_i+3b_i\le6x_i$. Their addition to the higher-dimensional exact search is ongoing; no four-part theorem follows merely from the availability of this template.

### 7.73 The two-fixed-type theorem no longer needs intersectingness [C]

**Theorem 7.71.** Let $a,b$ be two fixed admissible vectors of the same positive rank $r$, on any finite number of parts of positive capacities $x_i$. If the continuous transversal coefficient of the type-closed family with types $a,b$ exceeds $3r/4$, the family admits a continuous bad seven-tuple. Thus the $3/4$ upper threshold holds for every two-fixed-type family, including nonintersecting ones. Rational parameters admit a rational witness and integral realizations at suitable multiples.

This removes the intersecting hypothesis from Theorem 7.10. It does not allow either fixed vector to range over a convex component, and it does not address arbitrary set families.

*Transversal formula and the nonintersecting reduction.* Normalize $r=1$. To disable the component of type $a$, one must leave some coordinate below $a_i$, with $a_i>0$. The infimum cost is $x_i-a_i$. Consequently the union of the two components has coefficient
$$\tau^*=\min_{i:a_i>0,\ j:b_j>0}
\begin{cases}
x_i-\min(a_i,b_i),&i=j,\\
x_i-a_i+x_j-b_j,&i\ne j.
\end{cases}$$
The formula follows in both directions: the indicated coordinate deficits disable both components, and any residual capacity vector that disables both must have one such deficient coordinate for each. Strict deficits do not change the infimum.

If the family is intersecting, Theorem 7.10 applies. Otherwise one of $2a\le x$, $2b\le x$, or $a+b\le x$ holds coordinatewise. The first two conditions immediately permit a homogeneous Fano tuple, since $7a/4\le x$ or $7b/4\le x$. It remains to assume
$$a+b\le x.$$

We use four preliminary bad-tuple constructions. A Fano tuple with six rows of type $a$ and one of type $b$ is possible if $3a/2+b/4\le x$; the row bound $b\le x$ is already automatic. This is the one-versus-six capacity formula from Lemma 7.63. Its mirror is also available. A second six-versus-one construction is possible if $6a/5+b\le x$: in each part, allocate mass $a_i/5$ to each of the six cells consisting of five of the first six rows, and mass $b_i$ to the seventh row alone. Every first-six row has load $a_i$, but they have no common point, and their points are disjoint from the seventh row. No pair pierces the tuple. Again the mirrored construction is available.

If all four fail, choose witness coordinates $I,J,K,L$ with
$$x_I<\tfrac32a_I+\tfrac14b_I,\qquad
x_J<\tfrac14a_J+\tfrac32b_J,$$
$$x_K<\tfrac65a_K+b_K,\qquad
x_L<a_L+\tfrac65b_L.$$
Because $a+b\le x$, the first inequality forces $a_I>3b_I/2$, and the second forces $b_J>3a_J/2$. Thus $I\ne J$. The last two force $a_K>0$ and $b_L>0$. Retain only these at most four coordinates, label $I=0,J=1$, and record each coordinate's state as A ($a>0,b=0$), B ($a=0,b>0$), ab ($a\ge b>0$), or ba ($b\ge a>0$). The retained type sums are at most one, and all transversal inequalities from the displayed formula still hold strictly above $3/4$ on retained coordinates.

There are exactly 125 coordinate-identification/support/order cases: use $p=2,3,4$, require $\{0,1,K,L\}=[p]$, put coordinate 0 in state A or ab and coordinate 1 in state B or ba, and require the stated positive entries at $K,L$. In each case introduce a common margin $\gamma>0$ below all positive entries and all strict inequality gaps. This is possible because only finitely many quantities are involved. The case becomes a rational linear system: nonnegative variables, retained type sums at most one, $a+b\le x$, the support/order conditions, every retained-coordinate transversal inequality at least $3/4+\gamma$, and the four failure inequalities with margin $\gamma$.

Exact dual certificates show that 120 cases are infeasible or force $\gamma\le0$. The only cases requiring refinement have $p=2$:
$$ (K,L;\text{states})=(0,0;\mathrm{ab},\mathrm B),\ (0,0;\mathrm{ab},\mathrm{ba}),\
 (0,1;\mathrm{ab},\mathrm{ba}),\ (1,1;\mathrm A,\mathrm{ba}),\ (1,1;\mathrm{ab},\mathrm{ba}).$$

*Complete refinement.* The recursive proof uses just three additional certified capacity functions:
$$U(s,t)=\max\{5s/6+t,\ s+3t/4,\ 4s/3\},\qquad U(t,s),$$
$$V(s,t)=\max\{s/2+5t/4,\ s+t\}.$$
Their explicit bad supports, colourings, rational primal/dual capacity certificates, and direct no-covering-pair checks are in `logs/astra_two_type_recursive/templates.json`. Each function is therefore a sufficient construction over every number of parts, independently of the completeness of the 42-function catalogue.

At a positive-margin node, select one of these constructions. A counterexample must violate one of its defining linear forms at some coordinate. That coordinate is either already retained, or is one new coordinate with one of the four support/order states. A zero-zero coordinate cannot violate a nonnegative capacity bound. Branching over these possibilities is exhaustive. Keep the selected failure inequality and all earlier ones; after adding a coordinate, rebuild the type-sum and all transversal inequalities. A positive common margin still exists if the actual counterexample satisfies that branch.

The complete refinement has six branching nodes and 101 leaves, 107 nodes in total. Every leaf has an exact dual proving infeasibility or $\gamma\le0$. These exhaust the five remaining root cases. Therefore no counterexample with $a+b\le x$ exists. Combining this with the intersecting case and the homogeneous constructions proves the theorem. $\square$
