It verifies that every existing/new-coordinate, support-state and facet alternative occurs exactly once, that children retain their parents' assumptions, and that all 101 leaf duals are valid rational contradictions. All checks pass using only the standard library. The discovery programs are `p644_disjoint_two_types.py` and `p644_two_type_recursive.py`; no numerical status is used as a theorem certificate. The earlier 87-case intersecting certificate is needed for the other branch of the theorem.

### 7.74 Exact limit of adapting only the final request

**Lemma 7.72.** Consider the unrestricted continuous avoidance game after some edges with empty common intersection have been observed. Their candidate piercing pairs form complete products along a finite simple graph $G$ on positive-mass Venn cells; omit isolated cells. Every response has mass $r$ and may use fresh points outside the observed edges. Let $T<r$. Two remaining requests of mass at most $T$, with the second allowed to depend on the first response, can force a bad tuple if and only if two sets of mass at most $T$ chosen simultaneously already cover every candidate pair. Thus, in this unrestricted model, adapting only the final request does not improve the two-request finishing budget of Lemma 7.67.

*Proof.* The reverse implication is immediate. For the forward implication, fix the first request $D$ of a putative adaptive winning strategy. Let $m_i>0$ be the cell masses, and let $d_i$ be the mass of $D$ in cell $i$. Points of $D$ outside the candidate cells cannot help against the unrestricted adversary, which can always use fresh points. Put
$$F=\{i:d_i=m_i\},\qquad R=V(G)\setminus F,$$
and let $N(R)$ be the union of the graph neighborhoods of vertices in $R$. Unlike the anticomplete-neighborhood notation of Lemma 7.67, $N(R)$ here means ordinary neighbors. Write $I=R\setminus N(R)$.

An adversarial response can meet every cell of $R$ in arbitrarily small positive mass, meet no cell of $F$, and fill the rest of its rank with fresh points. More generally let its mass in cell $i$ be $h_i$, with $0\le h_i\le m_i-d_i$ and $\sum_i h_i\le r$. For responses positive in every $R$-cell, the union $K$ of endpoints of surviving candidate pairs has mass
$$|K|=m(N(R))+\sum_{i\in I}h_i.$$
Indeed, if a cell has a response point in a neighboring cell, all of its points remain endpoints of candidate pairs. If it has no response neighbor, exactly its own response points remain endpoints. The resulting supremum is
$$\sup |K|=m(N(R))+\min\left(r,\sum_{i\in I}(m_i-d_i)\right).$$
The formula remains valid when the supremum is approached by letting the required positive masses in other $R$-cells tend to zero. If $R$ is empty, $D$ already contains all candidate cells and the conclusion is immediate.

The final request must contain every point of $K$. If it omits an endpoint of a surviving candidate pair, the next response may include that endpoint and otherwise use fresh points, preserving a piercing pair. Therefore a winning strategy requires $\sup|K|\le T$. In particular $m(N(R))\le T$. Also $m(F)\le T$ and
$$\sum_{i\in I}(m_i-d_i)\ge \max\{0,m(I)+m(F)-T\}.$$
Because $T<r$, the rank truncation in the supremum cannot conceal a violation of the required bound. We obtain
$$m(F)\le T,\qquad m(N(R))\le T,\qquad m(N(R))+m(I)+m(F)\le2T.$$
The last inequality follows directly when $m(I)+m(F)>T$; otherwise it follows from $m(N(R))\le T$.

Now use the anticomplete pair
$$A=R,\qquad B=V(G)\setminus N(R).$$
Its common-request set in Lemma 7.67 is $C=N(R)\setminus R$. The two fixed loads there are exactly $m(N(R))$ and $m(F)$; its total-load condition is
$$m(V(G))+m(C)=m(N(R))+m(I)+m(F)\le2T.$$
All three conditions of Lemma 7.67 hold, so two simultaneous requests of mass at most $T$ cover all candidate pairs. This proves the forward implication. $\square$

This is a hand obstruction for the unrestricted response model, not for responses required to satisfy every additional global property of a hypothetical extremal family. Intersection gaps, minimum-good-triple restrictions and a bounded outside reservoir may prevent the adversarial responses used in the proof. Consequently later adaptivity remains useful only if it exploits such extra information, or if it begins before the last two requests. The strict budget gap in a continuous losing instance gives the corresponding obstruction at sufficiently large integral scales after rational approximation; no equality-case integer assertion is needed here.

### 7.75 The three-part two-box theorem without intersectingness [C]

**Theorem 7.73.** The continuous type-closed family of a union of at most two nonempty rank-$r$ sliced boxes over three parts has a bad seven-tuple whenever its continuous transversal coefficient exceeds $3r/4$. No intersectingness assumption is required. With rational capacities and box bounds, a rational witness exists and scales to integral witnesses at suitable multiples.

*Proof.* Normalize $r=1$. The intersecting case is Theorem 7.59. If one component contains disjoint types, their midpoint is an admissible type at most $x/2$ coordinatewise. It consequently fits the homogeneous Fano construction, whose capacity is $7a/4$. We may therefore assume each component is self-intersecting. In the remaining nonintersecting case there are $a$ in the first component and $b$ in the second with $a+b\le x$.

Use the canonical endpoints, capacity truncation $x_i\le2$, blocker formula and thirteen support orbits from the proof of Theorem 7.59. Truncation preserves a mixed-disjoint witness because every sum $a_i+b_i$ is at most two. It preserves the high-transversal condition by the same deletion argument. Every construction used below has per-part capacity at most $11/5$ on the square $[0,1]^2$, but preservation of its feasibility under truncation is not needed here: a bad tuple in the truncated capacities also fits the original capacities.

The mathematical systems retain the 36 transversal disjunctions and the self-intersection disjunction for each component. They also require failure of the homogeneous Fano construction in each component. Replace the previous strict mixed-intersection disjunction by the weak conditions for existence of a mixed-disjoint pair. In the polygon projection of §7.62 these are exactly $f\le0$ for every failure form $f$ of the coupling $s+t\le x$. Weak inequalities are essential: a disjoint pair is allowed to fill a part exactly.

In addition to both orientations of the earlier $M_1,M_5,M_{4,3}$ and noncollinear Fano construction, require failure of the following sufficient constructions and their mirrors:
$$M_{K_4}(s,t)=\max(2s/3+t,4s/3+t/2),\qquad D(s,t)=6s/5+t,$$
$$U(s,t)=\max(5s/6+t,s+3t/4,4s/3),\qquad V(s,t)=\max(s/2+5t/4,s+t).$$
The first has the hand proof in Lemma 7.70; $D$ has the six-versus-one disjoint construction in §7.73; the rational support certificates for $U,V$ are checked there independently. All the two-variable polygon projections are complete by the argument in §7.62. Thus every hypothetical counterexample satisfies one of the thirteen finite rational systems with a positive common margin.

All thirteen systems are inconsistent. The independent script `p644_two_box_general_audit.py --mixed` reconstructs every original assertion, including the weak mixed-disjointness inequalities, and matches every assumption in the contradiction proofs. The second solver cvc5 produced CPC proofs for all thirteen cases; standalone Ethos checked every one. Their mathematical input files, cores and proofs are in `logs/astra_two_box_general_3_mixed/`. The last three cases $033,123,333$ all passed; no timeout is treated as a proof. The original intersecting certificate is needed for the other branch of the theorem. This proves the continuous statement. Rational LP feasibility and row trimming give the stated rational and integral witnesses. $\square$

An auxiliary acceleration, `p644_box_linear_prune.py`, deletes disjuncts only after reconstructing exact rational Farkas certificates. Its independent replay `p644_box_linear_prune_check.py` verifies 1708, 1772 and 1460 deletions in cases $033,123,333$. The reduced-input solver runs timed out, so these are a checked acceleration experiment, not an additional theorem. The completed theorem above uses the independently checked original systems.

### 7.76 A gap lemma for arbitrary closed two-part type sets

Normalize rank to one. Let the two part capacities be $x,y>0$, let $N=x+y$, and let $C\subseteq[\max(0,1-y),\min(1,x)]$ be a nonempty closed set of admissible first-part sizes. Put $l=\min C$, $c=\max C$. No convexity is assumed.

The following elementary transversal bounds hold:
$$\tau^*\le N-1,\qquad \tau^*\le x-l\ (l>0),\qquad \tau^*\le y-1+c\ (c<1).$$
If $(u,v)\subseteq[l,c]$ is a gap of $C$, then
$$\tau^*\le N-1-(v-u).$$
Indeed, retaining first-part mass just below $v$ and second-part mass just below $1-u$ leaves no allowed type. Taking the infimum of the deletion costs proves the gap bound. The endpoint bounds follow by retaining just less than the required minimum in one part; the first bound follows by retaining total mass just below one.

**Lemma 7.74.** Suppose $\tau^*>3/4$ and there is no bad seven-tuple using at most two distinct admissible types. Set $\delta=N-7/4$. Then $\delta>0$, $x,y<7/4$, and there are $a,b\in C$ with
$$l\le a<b\le c,\qquad a<1-4y/7,\qquad b>4x/7,\qquad b-a<\delta.$$
Moreover
$$c-l<2\delta.$$

*Proof.* The homogeneous Fano construction excludes every type in
$$H=[1-4y/7,4x/7].$$
Its length is $4\delta/7>0$. There must be types on both sides. If all types lie above $H$, then $l>4x/7$ and
$$\tau^*\le x-l<3l/4\le3/4.$$
If all lie below $H$, the analogous bound is $\tau^*\le y-1+c<3(1-c)/4\le3/4$. Both contradict the hypothesis. Compactness now supplies the largest type $a$ below $H$ and the smallest type $b$ above it. They satisfy the displayed strict inequalities, which also imply $x,y<7/4$. The open interval $(a,b)$ misses $C$, so the gap bound gives $b-a<\delta$.

For any fixed $t\in C$, the one-versus-six Fano construction admits a partner $s\in C$ whenever
$$7-4y\le s+6t\le4x.$$
Thus the interval $I_t=[7-4y-6t,4x-6t]$, of length $4\delta$, misses $C$. It cannot intersect $[l,c]$: if it crossed either endpoint, it would contain an admissible type; if it lay between the endpoints, its length would contradict the gap bound. Consequently
$$t<\frac{7-4y-c}{6}\quad\hbox{or}\quad t>\frac{4x-l}{6}.$$
Therefore $C$ misses the interval
$$J=\left[\frac{7-4y-c}{6},\frac{4x-l}{6}\right],\qquad |J|=\frac{4\delta+c-l}{6}>0.$$
This interval cannot lie to the left of $l$: that would give $4x<7l$ and the same endpoint contradiction $\tau^*<3l/4$. Nor can it lie to the right of $c$, by the symmetric endpoint contradiction. Since its endpoints cannot cross $l$ or $c$, it lies in $(l,c)$. The gap bound yields $|J|<\delta$, or $c-l<2\delta$, as required. $\square$

The lemma uses actual gaps of the admissible set. It does not fill those gaps or assume that intermediate types are present. This is what permits the next theorem to go beyond unions of two intervals.

### 7.77 The $3/4$ threshold for every closed two-part type set [C]

**Theorem 7.75.** Let $C$ be any nonempty closed admissible type set over two parts. If the continuous type-closed family has $\tau^*>3r/4$, it contains a continuous bad seven-tuple using at most two distinct types. Neither convexity nor intersectingness is assumed. One of the 42 certified supports in Theorem 7.69 suffices; each has at most fourteen parent cells.

*Proof and exact certificate.* Normalize $r=1$ and suppose no such tuple exists. Lemma 7.74 supplies $x,y,l,c,a,b$ and the strict inequalities stated there. Add the endpoint transversal bounds whenever $l>0$ and $c<1$. Split into the four cases specifying whether $l=0$ and whether $c=1$. Part exchange
$$(x,y,l,c,a,b)\longmapsto(y,x,1-c,1-l,1-b,1-a)$$
interchanges the two cases with exactly one pure endpoint; it is enough to treat cases $00,10,11$, where the first digit indicates $l=0$ and the second indicates $c=1$.

For each certified capacity function $M(s,t)=\max_j(u_js+v_jt)$, and each ordered pair $s,t$ of the four actual types $l,a,b,c$, failure of its construction means that at least one of
$$u_js+v_jt-x>0,\qquad u_j(1-s)+v_j(1-t)-y>0$$
holds. All conditions are finite disjunctions of rational linear inequalities. A common margin $\gamma>0$ below the positive gaps converts them into weak linear inequalities. The underlying variables are $(x,y,l,c,\gamma,a,b)$, with $x,y\le7/4$, $l\ge0$, $c\le1$, $c\le x$, $1-l\le y$ and the order conditions from the lemma. Any hypothetical counterexample satisfies these systems.

The discovery search selected small subsets of these valid assumptions: sixteen assertions for $00$, fourteen for $10$, and nineteen for $11$. After exact Boolean normalization their disjunction sizes are respectively $(4,4,4)$, $(4,4,4)$ and $(2,4,2,8,4)$. Expanding these gives exactly $64+64+512=640$ rational linear systems. Every one is inconsistent with $\gamma>0$.

For a system $Av\le b$ with the seven variables treated as free, the certificate provides a sparse rational vector $z\le0$. It either satisfies
$$z^TA=0,\qquad z^Tb>0,$$
which is an immediate contradiction, or
$$z^TA=-e_\gamma^T,\qquad z^Tb\ge0,$$
which forces $\gamma\le0$. The strict assertion $\gamma>0$ is relaxed to $\gamma\ge0$ only while producing this upper-bound certificate; the resulting conclusion still excludes every positive margin. Equality of coefficient vectors is checked exactly, so no unstated sign assumption on a variable is needed.

`p644_two_part_gap_check.py` independently reconstructs all permitted mathematical assumptions and verifies that each saved core is a subset. It enumerates the full Cartesian product of its alternatives, checks all 640 rational duals, and directly checks every construction's bad support, row colours, primal/dual capacity witnesses and fourteen-parent bound. Its construction audit needs only these explicit positive witnesses, not completeness of the large 715-support catalogue. It imports no numerical solver or discovery module. Replay passes with
```
python3 -B -S p644_two_part_gap_check.py
```
The data are `logs/astra_two_part_gap_central/{templates.json,exact_duals.json,00.core.smt2,10.core.smt2,11.core.smt2}`. Discovery used `p644_two_part_gap_pipeline.py` and `p644_two_part_gap_duals.py`; a separate cvc5/Ethos run also checked contradictions for all four endpoint cases, but is unnecessary for the 640-dual replay.

Every possible counterexample has therefore been eliminated. The successful construction supplies a bad tuple using one or two actual admissible types. The homogeneous Fano and one-versus-six constructions used in Lemma 7.74 also have at most fourteen parent cells. This proves the theorem. $\square$

The theorem is continuous for arbitrary closed real $C$. Rational capacities and a finite set of rational types give rational witnesses. No rationality assertion is made for an arbitrary closed set containing only irrational types. The following finite consequence avoids any limiting assumption on the sequence of type sets.

**Corollary 7.76 (uniform finite two-part bound).** Let $\mathcal H$ be a $k$-uniform family invariant under every permutation within each of two disjoint parts of its ground set. If $\mathcal H$ has property $(7,2)$, then
$$\tau(\mathcal H)\le\lfloor3k/4\rfloor+28.$$
The admissible integer first-part sizes may be completely arbitrary.

*Proof.* For an integer two-part type family, its finite transversal number is at most its continuous coefficient plus two. To see this, round down both coordinates of any continuous free residual box. The resulting integer residual box is still free, and the deletion cost increases by less than two. Taking infima gives the stated inequality.

Delete thirteen vertices from each part, or the entire part if it has fewer than thirteen vertices. Let $\mathcal H'$ consist of the original edges avoiding those deleted vertices. It is still type-closed, its rank is still $k$, and
$$\tau(\mathcal H')\ge\tau(\mathcal H)-26.$$
Indeed a transversal of $\mathcal H'$ together with the deleted vertices hits every original edge. If $\tau(\mathcal H)>3k/4+28$, it follows that the continuous coefficient of $\mathcal H'$ exceeds $3k/4$.

Apply Theorem 7.75 to its finite closed set of integer type vectors. It gives seven row types and a bad parent support with at most fourteen cells, together with nonnegative real parent masses in each part. Round each parent mass up to an integer. The total mass in a part increases by less than fourteen, hence the new integer total is at most the integer remaining capacity plus thirteen. If a remaining part has capacity zero, all its masses were zero and remain zero; otherwise thirteen deleted vertices are available. Thus the rounded construction fits in the original capacities. Its loads dominate the prescribed row sizes, which are integers. Remove membership from each row until its two sizes are exactly its prescribed type. This can be done with integer points, independently for each row. Trimming only replaces parent cells by subsets, so it cannot introduce a pair covering all seven rows.

The resulting seven edges belong to the original type-closed family and are not two-pierceable, a contradiction. If only one part survives the deletion, the same argument uses the homogeneous Fano construction for the resulting one-part complete family; if no edge survives, the assumed transversal inequality was already impossible. We conclude $\tau(\mathcal H)\le3k/4+28$, and integrality gives the displayed bound. $\square$

This proves the conjectured leading coefficient for all two-part type-closed families, uniformly even when their allowed type sets change with $k$. The missing reduction is from arbitrary set families to such symmetry or to an equally strong structural substitute. No such reduction is supplied, and the general bound remains $c_7\le6/7$.

### 7.78 A higher-dimensional partner test and a precise limitation

**Lemma 7.77 (partner-box test).** Let a rank-$r$ type-closed family have continuous coefficient greater than $T$, and let $b$ be an actual admissible type. Let
$$M(s,t)=\max_j(u_js+v_jt),\qquad u_j,v_j\ge0,$$
be any sufficient two-type bad-tuple capacity. Suppose $v_jb_i\le x_i$ whenever $u_j=0$, and define
$$h_i=\min\left(x_i,\ \min_{j:u_j>0}\frac{x_i-v_jb_i}{u_j}\right).$$
If $h_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i(x_i-h_i)\le T$, there is a bad seven-tuple.

*Proof.* The residual box with capacities $h$ cannot be free, since its deletion cost is at most $T<\tau^*$. It therefore contains an admissible type $a\le h$. Every facet of $M$ satisfies $u_ja_i+v_jb_i\le x_i$, including the facets with $u_j=0$. Applying the certified construction independently in each part gives the bad tuple. $\square$

One possible extension of the two-part argument would discard every type excluded by this test, then find a transversal of cost $3r/4$ for all the survivors. The following shows that this single round of tests is insufficient even with the complete 42-function two-type menu.

**Proposition 7.78 [C].** At rank one and capacities $x=(4/5,4/5,4/5)$, let
$$C=\{b\in[0,4/5]^3:b_1+b_2+b_3=1,\ \max_i b_i\ge27/50\}.$$
The associated type-closed family has $\tau^*=39/50$. Every one of its types survives the homogeneous Fano exclusion and every partner-box test of Lemma 7.77 at budget $3/4$ using one of the 42 functions. Nevertheless this family has a bad tuple using two explicit types. Thus it is a counterexample to completeness of that one-round test, not a counterexample to Problem 644.

*Transversal calculation.* A residual vector $z\le x$ contains an admissible type precisely when $\sum z_i\ge1$ and some $z_i\ge27/50$. Necessity is immediate. For sufficiency allocate $27/50$ in that coordinate and distribute the remaining $23/50$ among the residual capacities, whose total is sufficient. Consequently a residual vector is free exactly when its total is below one or all its coordinates are below $27/50$. The supremum free total is
$$\max(1,81/50)=81/50,$$
so $\tau^*=12/5-81/50=39/50>3/4$.

*Exact obstruction certificate.* For each capacity function $M$, consider all vectors $b,h$ satisfying
$$0\le b_i,h_i\le4/5,\quad \sum_i b_i=1,\quad\sum_i h_i\ge33/20,$$
$$u_jh_i+v_jb_i\le4/5\qquad\text{for every part }i\text{ and every facet }j.$$
Any type admitting a partner box of cost at most $3/4$ occurs in this system. For each of the 42 functions an exact rational certificate proves that this system is infeasible, or that $b_1\le8/15$. The same bound holds for either other coordinate by permutation. There are 31 infeasibility certificates and 11 upper-bound certificates. Since
$$27/50>8/15,$$
no member of $C$ admits such a cheap partner box. Each member also has a coordinate exceeding $4(4/5)/7=16/35$, so it fails the homogeneous Fano capacity test.

The independent standard-library script `p644_partner_budget_barrier_check.py` reconstructs all 42 matrices, verifies their sparse rational dual inequalities, and directly checks the positive construction certificates. Data are `logs/astra_partner_budget_barrier.json` and the 42 construction records already used in §7.77. Discovery is `p644_partner_budget_barrier.py`. All exact checks pass; no numerical optimality flag is used.

For clarity, the family really does fail $(7,2)$. Take
$$a=(27/50,23/100,23/100),\qquad b=(23/100,27/50,23/100).$$
Both are admissible. Certified menu function 6 is
$$W(s,t)=\max(s/2+t,\ 9s/8+3t/4,\ 5s/4+t/2,\ 4s/3).$$
Its costs on the three parts are exactly $79/100$, $531/800$ and $69/160$, each strictly less than $4/5$. Its explicit support therefore gives a bad seven-tuple. These evaluations are also checked independently. $\square$

Since the survivor set contains $C$, it has coefficient at least $39/50$ and cannot be hit at cost $3/4$. A stronger argument must retain compatibility constraints between actual types, iterate with additional information, or exploit other consequences of high transversal number. The fixed-capacity discovery probes at $(2/3,2/3,2/3)$ and $(1/2,1/2,4/5)$ did find survivor covers; their SMT inputs are saved by `p644_partner_budget_probe.py`, but those isolated outputs have not received an independent proof audit and are not used by any theorem here.

### 7.79 Two actual types no longer suffice over three parts

The conclusion of Theorem 7.75 that a bad tuple can use at most two actual types is special to its two-part hypothesis. The next example gives an exact obstruction to that stronger conclusion in three parts, even when the complete two-type catalogue is used.

**Proposition 7.79 [C].** There is a three-part type-closed family of continuous rank one and coefficient $483/640>3/4$ such that every subfamily consisting of at most two admissible types has property $(7,2)$. The whole family fails $(7,2)$. At one integer scale it has rank $640$ and transversal number $486$.

*Construction and exact verification.* It is convenient first to use rank $80$ and three capacities $513/8$. The nine admissible vectors are
$$
\begin{array}{rrr}
0&54&26\\
1&62&17\\
8&43&29\\
19&0&61\\
28&1&51\\
31&4&45\\
44&32&4\\
51&29&0\\
58&21&1
\end{array}.
$$
For every ordered pair $s,t$ of these vectors and every one of the 42 complete capacity functions $M(s,t)=\max_j(u_js+v_jt)$ of Theorem 7.69, the checker evaluates
$$\max_{i,j}(u_js_i+v_jt_i-513/8).$$
All $9^2\cdot42=3402$ quantities are positive; their minimum is exactly $1/8$. Completeness of Theorem 7.69 therefore excludes every continuous bad tuple using at most two of these types. In particular it excludes integer bad tuples in each two-type subfamily at every feasible scale.

To compute the transversal coefficient independently of the discovery code, assign each of the nine types a coordinate in which it will be blocked. A coordinate can block a type only when that type has positive mass there. For an assignment, the supremum residual mass in a used coordinate is the least assigned type coordinate; an unused coordinate retains its full capacity. Exhausting these at most $3^9$ assignments gives maximum residual total $132$, attained as a supremum at $(58,29,45)$. Hence
$$\tau^*=3(513/8)-132=483/8,$$
or $483/640$ after rank normalization. These assignments are exhaustive because each free residual box must fail to dominate every allowed type in at least one coordinate.

Multiplying all data by eight gives rank $640$, capacities $513$, and integer type coordinates. In the same blocking calculation, each used residual threshold is now one less than the least assigned integer type coordinate. The maximum integer free total is $1053$, attained at $(463,231,359)$. Thus the exact finite transversal number is $1539-1053=486$.

For a positive witness that the whole family is not $(7,2)$, label the nine displayed types $0,\ldots,8$. On the Fano lines of Lemma 7.63 choose the seven row labels
$$(4,2,1,4,8,8,1).$$
The three exact parent-capacity costs are $117/2$, $63$, and $103/2$, all below $513/8$. Lemma 7.63 and row trimming give a continuous bad tuple involving four distinct actual types. This is a Fano **parent** construction; trimmed cells need not all have degree four. Independently, the certificate supplies 22 integer cells at rank $640$, with row labels $(1,1,3,4,7,8,8)$. Their three part totals are all $513$, every row has its prescribed type, and no two positive cells have union $[7]$.

The standard-library checker `p644_three_part_two_type_barrier_check.py` verifies every pair exclusion, both exhaustive transversal calculations, both positive witnesses, and the fact that deleting any one of these nine types removes this example's strict excess above $3/4$. Data are `logs/astra_three_part_two_type_barrier.json`, its `.fano.json` companion, and the 42-function table. Replay passes with `python3 -B -S p644_three_part_two_type_barrier_check.py`. The assertion that the 42 tests exclude **all** two-type bad tuples uses the separately certified completeness theorem; the small checker does not replace that catalogue proof. $\square$

Thus keeping arbitrarily many actual responses while checking only pairs cannot prove the three-part analogue of Theorem 7.75. The example is a precise obstruction to that information restriction, not to the desired $3/4$ bound for $(7,2)$-families. Searches must also use tuples involving at least three distinct types, or additional structural information.

### 7.80 A continuous theorem from whole type cells

**Theorem 7.80 [C].** Let a type-closed family have rank $r$ and three parts, each of capacity $4r/5$. Its admissible type set can be arbitrary. If its continuous transversal coefficient exceeds $3r/4$, it has a continuous bad seven-tuple. No convexity or intersectingness is assumed.

This is a fixed-capacity result. It is neither the theorem for all three-part capacities nor a reduction of arbitrary families to three parts. In particular, it does not change the unrestricted coefficient $6/7$.

*Reduction to a finite, exact certificate.* Scale to rank $40$ and capacities $(32,32,32)$, with target transversal cost $30$. Partition the type polygon into the closed unit triangles
$$P_l=\{a:l_i\le a_i\le l_i+1,\ \sum_i a_i=40\},$$
where $l$ is integral, $\sum l_i$ is $39$ or $38$, and every vertex lies in $[0,32]^3$. These triangles cover the entire type polygon, including its boundary: they are the two orientations of the usual triangular lattice in the plane $\sum a_i=40$. Overlap on boundaries causes no problem.

Discard any triangle whose coordinate maximum $h=l+(1,1,1)$ satisfies $7h_i\le128$ for all $i$. Every type in such a triangle has a homogeneous Fano bad tuple, so under the contrary hypothesis no admissible type belongs to it. There remain exactly $1212$ triangles. Introduce a Boolean variable for each, true when it contains an actual admissible type.

For each integer vector $u\in[0,32]^3$ with $\sum u_i=66$, the deletion cost is $30$. The assumption $\tau^*>30$ supplies an admissible type $a\le u$. Therefore at least one triangle meeting this residual box is occupied. A triangle meets it exactly when
$$l_i\le u_i\quad\text{for all }i,\qquad \sum_i\min(h_i,u_i)\ge40.$$
These conditions follow by filling the coordinate intervals $[l_i,\min(h_i,u_i)]$ to total $40$. The resulting $496$ positive clauses are valid for every admissible set, not just for grid-valued types.

If a certified two-type capacity function fits the two coordinate maxima of two triangles, then any actual types in those triangles give a bad tuple by monotonicity and row trimming. This supplies the pair exclusions. Only positive construction certificates are needed here; completeness of the 42-function menu is not used.

The remaining exclusions use several types. A region is a set of triangles whose coordinate maxima lie below a rational vector $b$. For each saved list of such regions, seven row labels specify which region supplies each row. In $551$ cases the Fano-parent inequalities of Lemma 7.63 verify the construction. In the other five cases explicit rational masses on a bad parent support verify every row demand and the three capacity bounds. Choosing one actual type from each occupied region then gives a bad tuple. Consequently those regions cannot all be occupied. Auxiliary Boolean variables express that occupation of any member triangle forces occupation of its region. Every implication and every forbidden combination is supplied explicitly.

The resulting formula has $3032$ variables and $538035$ clauses. `p644_continuous_type_cells_check.py` reconstructs the triangular lattice independently from its vertices, checks the full residual-query list, checks all positive capacity certificates, verifies the rational region constructions, and reproduces every clause in order. It imports no solver or discovery module. The input audit passes.

An independent RUP-only LRAT certificate then proves the formula inconsistent. The small standard-library checker `p644_lrat_rup_check.py` replays $74164$ derived clauses and $11471059$ exact unit-propagation steps, ending in the empty clause. It rejects RAT steps and uses no SAT solver. Both this replay and the separate DRAT-trim/LRAT-check replays pass. The original incremental SAT output is not needed: the delivered proof is a fresh proof for the fully assembled, independently audited formula.

Thus an admissible set with coefficient exceeding $30$ cannot avoid a bad tuple. Rescaling proves the theorem. Rational capacities and finitely many rational admissible types yield rational witnesses and hence integer bad tuples at suitable multiples; no stronger uniform integer-rounding statement is asserted here. $\square$

Data have prefix `logs/astra_continuous_type_cells/40_32_32_32_T30_fano_regions_parents`, with the `.json`, `.cnf`, and `.lrat` files used in verification. The LRAT file may be losslessly gzip-compressed for replay. Discovery tools are `p644_continuous_type_cells.py`, `p644_fano_type_assignment.py`, and `p644_parent_type_assignment.py`. The external checker source is the primary repository `https://github.com/marijnheule/drat-trim`, commit `2e3b2dc0ecf938addbd779d42877b6ed69d9a985`; its code is not a dependency of the standard-library proof replay.

The distinction from a grid scan is essential: each node contains an entire triangle, pair and multi-type exclusions hold throughout those triangles, and residual-box clauses permit every triangle that can meet the box. A satisfiable relaxation would be inconclusive. An independently verified contradiction proves the continuous assertion.

### 7.81 A global cover potential and a one-exchange obstruction

For a tuple $\mathcal F$ with empty common intersection, write
$$P(\mathcal F)=\{x:\text{some two-point transversal of }\mathcal F\text{ contains }x\}.$$
This set lies in the union of the tuple's edges. If $\mathcal F$ has at most six edges in a $(7,2)$-family $\mathcal H$, then $P(\mathcal F)$ is a transversal of $\mathcal H$: a pair piercing $\mathcal F\cup\{E\}$ has at least one point in $E$, and that point belongs to $P(\mathcal F)$. Thus minimizing $|P(\mathcal F)|$ over six-edge tuples with empty common intersection is a possible global potential, rather than an assumption of symmetry within parts.

The following shows that minimality of this potential alone cannot yield a one-exchange argument at any asymptotic budget below the full edge size. It holds even when all displayed edges are distinct and pairwise intersecting.

**Lemma 7.81 (hand obstruction).** For every integer $k\ge4$, there are six distinct, pairwise intersecting $k$-edges with empty common intersection and $|P|=2k-6$ such that the following holds. For every requested deletion set $D$ of size at most $k-4$, one can choose a further $k$-edge $G$ disjoint from $D$ so that all seven edges are distinct and pairwise intersecting, the seven are two-pierceable, every six have empty common intersection, and every six-edge eligible-point set has size at least $2k-6$. Fresh outside points are allowed.

*Proof.* Take disjoint sets $A,B$ of size $k-3$, and nine further points $x_{ij}$ for $1\le i,j\le3$. Define
$$E_i=A\cup\{x_{i1},x_{i2},x_{i3}\},\qquad F_j=B\cup\{x_{1j},x_{2j},x_{3j}\}.$$
Each edge has size $k$. Edges in one group meet in their common core, and $E_i\cap F_j=\{x_{ij}\}$, so the six edges are distinct and pairwise intersecting. Their common intersection is empty.

Every pair consisting of one point of $A$ and one of $B$ covers all six. No cross point $x_{ij}$ is eligible: it covers only $E_i,F_j$, and no point covers the other four edges. Indeed a core point belongs to three original edges, and a cross point to two. A point outside their union is also ineligible, because the six edges have no common point. Hence $P=A\cup B$ and $|P|=2k-6$.

Since $|D|\le k-4<|A|=|B|$, choose $a\in A\setminus D$ and $b\in B\setminus D$. Complete $\{a,b\}$ to a $k$-set $G$ using $k-2$ fresh points outside $D$ and all the old edges. Then $G$ meets every $E_i$ at $a$ and every $F_j$ at $b$, and $\{a,b\}$ pierces all seven edges. The fresh points also make $G$ distinct from the original edges.

Every point of $A$ can be paired with $b$ to cover all seven, and every point of $B$ can be paired with $a$. Thus every six-edge eligible-point set contains $A\cup B$. Finally, each point belongs to at most four of the seven edges, so every six have empty common intersection. This proves all assertions. $\square$

This is a finite response obstruction. It does not assert that the displayed seven-edge family extends to a high-transversal $(7,2)$-family: in fact these seven edges have a common two-point transversal. It shows that an argument using only the initial eligible-cover value, its nondecrease under one exchange, pairwise intersection, and one avoidance request cannot exclude this state. Further consequences of high transversal number, or several exchanges, are essential.

`p644_eligible_exchange_check.py` independently checks the incidence, pairwise intersections, eligible-point sets and all seven sixfold intersections at five ranks. The proof above is uniform in $k$ and in $D$. A preceding, weaker Fano-based obstruction remains reproducible in `p644_eligible_exchange_fano_check.py`; it is not needed for this lemma.

### 7.82 Retaining the number of piercing pairs gives a different exchange lemma

The preceding obstruction discards the shape of the graph of piercing pairs. In its example, adding $G$ changes the complete bipartite graph between $A$ and $B$ into the union of two stars, even though its eligible vertex set stays unchanged. This suggests a different global potential.

For a tuple $\mathcal F$ with empty common intersection, let $Q(\mathcal F)$ be the number of unordered pairs of distinct points piercing every edge of $\mathcal F$. Both points of such a pair must belong to the union of the edges, so this number is finite and independent of unused ambient points. Under the large-transversal hypothesis below, a six-edge tuple with empty common intersection exists: choose two edges with intersection at most $k-T$ by avoiding a $T$-subset of the first, then choose a third avoiding their intersection, using $k-T\le T$. Repeating rows pads this good triple to six. Choose a tuple minimizing $Q$ among all six-edge tuples with empty common intersection.

**Lemma 7.82.** Suppose $\mathcal H$ is $k$-uniform, has property $(7,2)$, and $\tau(\mathcal H)>\lceil3k/4\rceil$. A six-edge tuple minimizing $Q$ among those with empty common intersection cannot have exactly the six-row Fano-complement atom pattern: seven disjoint atom classes labelled by the Fano points, with the six edges equal to the complements of six of the seven Fano lines within their union. Atom classes of size zero are allowed.

*Proof.* Let $L_0$ be the omitted line, with its three atom classes called $B$, and call the other four classes $A$. The six equal row sizes force all four $A$ classes to have one size $a$, and all three $B$ classes one size $b$. To see the first assertion, compare the two rows whose omitted lines meet $L_0$ at the same point. The sums on the two complementary pairs of $A$ labels agree. Doing this for the three perfect matchings on four labels gives all four $A$ sizes equal. Comparing the resulting row sizes gives equality of the three $B$ sizes. Thus
$$2a+2b=k.$$

The pairs piercing all six rows are precisely the pairs of points in different $B$ classes, so
$$Q(\mathcal F)=3b^2,\qquad P(\mathcal F)=B_1\cup B_2\cup B_3.$$
Since this eligible set is a transversal of $\mathcal H$, put $T=\lceil3k/4\rceil$ and obtain $3b>T$. Choose $D\subseteq B_1\cup B_2\cup B_3$ of size $T$, distributed as evenly as possible among the three classes. This is possible because $b\ge\lfloor T/3\rfloor+1$. The number of old piercing pairs with both endpoints in $D$ is
$$L=\left\lfloor T^2/3\right\rfloor.$$
Take $G\in\mathcal H$ avoiding $D$.

Omit any one original row, belonging to line $L_i\ne L_0$, and replace it by $G$. This new six-tuple still has empty common intersection: an original point lies in at most four old rows and at most five rows after adding $G$, and a fresh point lies only in $G$. A pair covering its five old rows cannot use a point outside the original union, because no original point belongs to five old rows. Nor can its two points have the same atom label. Two distinct Fano labels determine their unique missed line, so a pair covering those five rows must have both labels on $L_0$ or both on $L_i$.

At least $L$ of the old $3b^2$ pairs are lost, because both endpoints avoid $G$. The total number of possibly new pairs on $L_i$, which has two $A$ labels and one $B$ label, is at most
$$a^2+2ab=k^2/4-b^2.$$
Consequently
$$Q(\mathcal F_i)\le Q(\mathcal F)-L+k^2/4-b^2.$$

For completeness, the strict integer inequality needed here has no rounding gap. Write $T=3q+s$, $0\le s\le2$. Since $b\ge q+1$, the difference between $L+b^2$ and $4T^2/9$ is at least $2q+1$, $4q/3+5/9$, or $2q/3+2/9$ according as $s=0,1,2$. Each is positive. Since $T\ge3k/4$, this proves
$$L+b^2>4T^2/9\ge k^2/4.$$
It follows that $Q(\mathcal F_i)<Q(\mathcal F)$, contradicting the global minimal choice. $\square$

This is a conditional structural lemma for arbitrary families, not an assumption of type closure. It does not show that the minimizing six-tuple must have this pattern, or that it is close to it. The new open step is to exploit the same pair-count minimality for other six-row supports; replacing it by eligible-point cardinality loses precisely the information identified in Lemma 7.81.

### 7.83 Why pair-count minimality needs more than one exchange

There is another six-row pattern for which one exchange cannot decrease the stronger potential, regardless of the deletion set. This identifies a concrete next difficulty for the route in Lemma 7.82.

**Lemma 7.83 (hand obstruction).** For every integer $m\ge1$, put $k=10m$. There are six distinct, pairwise intersecting $k$-edges with empty common intersection and $Q=10m^2$ such that, for every $D$ of size at most $k-1$, an additional edge $G$ avoiding $D$ can be chosen with the following properties: all seven edges are distinct and pairwise intersecting; the seven are two-pierceable; every six have empty common intersection; and every six have at least $10m^2$ piercing pairs. The response uses only the original $2k$ points.

*Proof.* For each three-subset $S\subseteq[6]$ take an atom $X_S$ of size $m$, all twenty atoms disjoint. Let $U$ be their union and set
$$E_i=\bigcup_{S\ni i}X_S\qquad(1\le i\le6).$$
Each edge has $\binom52m=10m$ points, and each pair of edges intersects in $\binom41m=4m$ points. A point belongs to precisely three original edges. The pairs piercing all six are exactly the pairs with endpoints in complementary atoms $X_S,X_{S^c}$. There are ten such atom pairs, so $Q=10m^2$.

A deletion set meeting every such piercing pair must wholly delete at least one atom in each complementary pair, and hence has size at least $10m=k$. Therefore a set $D$ of size at most $k-1$ leaves two points $p\in X_S\setminus D$, $q\in X_{S^c}\setminus D$ for some complementary labels. Choose $G\subseteq U\setminus D$ of size $k$ containing $p,q$; there are enough available points because $|U|=2k$. The pair $\{p,q\}$ pierces all seven edges. Each original edge contains exactly one of $p,q$, so $G$ meets every original edge and is distinct from each of them. Every point belongs to at most four of the seven rows, so every six have empty common intersection.

It remains to prove the pair-count inequalities. In fact they hold for **every** $k$-subset $G$ of $U$, without using its particular choice. Put
$$u_S=|X_S\setminus G|,\qquad 0\le u_S\le m,\qquad\sum_Su_S=k=10m.$$
Omit row $E_j$. Pairs that cover the remaining five original rows have either complementary labels, or two labels with union $[6]\setminus\{j\}$. The latter labels both avoid $j$. On the ten three-subsets of a five-set, the relation that their union is the full five-set is a three-regular graph with fifteen edges: for one three-subset, its partner must contain its two missing elements and one of its three present elements.

Thus the graph of atom pairs covering those five rows consists of this three-regular graph on ten core vertices and the ten complementary matching edges to the other ten vertices, which are leaves. It has twenty-five edges in total. A point pair among these fails to pierce $G$ exactly when both endpoints avoid $G$. Therefore the new six-tuple has
$$Q_j=25m^2-\sum_{\{S,T\}\in J_j}u_Su_T.$$
On the core graph, $u_Su_T\le(u_S^2+u_T^2)/2$ and $u_S^2\le m u_S$ give a total of at most $(3m/2)\sum_{\rm core}u_S$. The matching contributes at most $m\sum_{\rm leaves}u_S$. Hence
$$\sum_{\{S,T\}\in J_j}u_Su_T
\le\frac{3m}{2}\sum_Su_S
=15m^2,$$
and $Q_j\ge10m^2$, as required. Omitting $G$ restores the original six-tuple. $\square$

The lemma does not construct a high-transversal $(7,2)$-family. Its seven displayed edges have a two-point transversal. It shows that even the full pair-count minimality, sixfold empty intersections and pairwise intersectingness do not force progress from a single avoidance response at any budget below $k$. A proof through this potential must use additional global restrictions or compare six-tuples involving several new responses. The latter is not ruled out: global minimality would constrain every such six-tuple, whereas this obstruction concerns only one new edge.

### 7.84 A complete second-response audit at a balanced state

The following is conditional on a particular first response. It does not say that this response can avoid every possible first request, so it is not a complete two-move adversary strategy.

**Proposition 7.84 [C].** In the construction of Lemma 7.83 let $m$ be even, and let $G_1$ contain exactly half the points of each of the twenty atoms. For every $k$-subset $H$ of $U$, the eight rows
$$E_1,\ldots,E_6,G_1,H$$
are two-pierceable, every six have empty common intersection, and every six have at least $10m^2$ piercing pairs. In particular, for any second request $D$ of size less than $k$, one can choose such an $H$ disjoint from $D$. It can also be chosen distinct from and intersecting every previous row.

*Proof, with an exact graph certificate.* Given any point $x\in H\cap X_S$, choose $y\in G_1\cap X_{S^c}$. The pair $x,y$ pierces all eight rows. Each point is in at most three of the original rows and at most five rows altogether, so no six have a common point.

Six-tuples not containing both $G_1$ and $H$ have the pair-count lower bound by Lemma 7.83. It remains to handle four original rows together with $G_1,H$. All fifteen choices of four original rows are equivalent by permutation of the six old labels. Fix rows $1,2,3,4$.

Split each atom into its half inside $G_1$ and its half outside $G_1$, giving forty classes of size $m/2$. Form a graph $J$ on these classes: two are adjacent when a pair from them covers the four fixed old rows and $G_1$. Its definition involves only their six-row labels and their $G_1$ membership. It has exactly $138$ edges, and no within-class pairs qualify. Let $u_i$ be the number of points of class $i$ outside $H$. Then
$$0\le u_i\le m/2,\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{40}u_i=10m,$$
and the new six-tuple has pair count
$$Q=138(m/2)^2-\sum_{ij\in E(J)}u_i u_j.$$
Writing $v_i=2u_i/m$ gives $0\le v_i\le1$ and $\sum v_i=20$. Since $v_i v_j\le\min(v_i,v_j)$, the lost-pair sum is bounded by $(m/2)^2$ times the optimum of
$$\max\sum_{ij\in E(J)}z_{ij},\qquad
0\le v_i,z_{ij}\le1,\quad\sum_i v_i\le20,\quad z_{ij}\le v_i,v_j.$$
An exact rational dual certificate gives upper bound $315/4$. Consequently
$$Q\ge\frac{m^2}{4}\left(138-\frac{315}{4}\right)
=\frac{237m^2}{16}>10m^2.$$

The checker `p644_balanced_pair_exchange_check.py` independently reconstructs all forty classes and all 138 graph edges, reconstructs every LP inequality, and verifies the 170 nonzero dual coefficients by exact rational arithmetic. Data are `logs/astra_balanced_pair_exchange_dual.json`; replay passes using only the standard library. This is an upper-bound certificate, so no numerical optimality assertion is used.

Finally, if $|D|<k$, the argument of Lemma 7.83 leaves an old piercing pair $p,q$ outside $D$. There is also a point of $G_1\setminus D$ and a point of $(U\setminus G_1)\setminus D$, since both halves have size $k$. Include these at most four points in $H$ and fill it inside $U\setminus D$ to size $k$. The old piercing pair ensures intersection with every old row and ensures $H$ is distinct from them; the other chosen points ensure intersection with $G_1$ and inequality to $G_1$. All the already proved conclusions hold for this $H$. $\square$

This exact audit replaces an unproductive enumeration. At rank $20$ and request size $15$, a response list intended to cover every request would need at least
$$\left\lceil\frac{\binom{40}{15}}{\binom{20}{15}}\right\rceil=2594514$$
distinct responses: one twenty-set is disjoint from only $\binom{20}{15}$ of the possible fifteen-set requests. The exploratory enumeration stopped at 2000 responses and was not an exhaustion. The small dual certificate proves the balanced-state assertion directly. A separate first response concentrated on ten whole atoms also survived 2000 request probes; that run remains inconclusive and is not covered by this proposition.

### 7.85 A disjoint-edge lower bound of $2/3$


**Proposition 7.85 (hand proof; priority unchecked).** Let $k,c$ be integers with $1\le c<2k/3$. Take disjoint sets $A,C,D$ with
\[
|A|=k,\qquad |C|=c,\qquad |D|=k-c,
\]
and put $U=A\cup C$, $B=C\cup D$. The $k$-uniform family
\[
\mathcal H=\binom Uk\cup\{B\}
\]
has property $(7,2)$, has disjoint edges $A,B$, and has transversal number exactly $c+1$.

*Transversal number.* The complete subfamily $\binom Uk$ has transversal number $|U|-k+1=c+1$, providing the lower bound. The set consisting of all $c$ points of $C$ and one point of $A$ meets every core edge and also $B$. This proves equality. The assumption $c\ge1$ is used here.

*Seven core edges.* Any two core edges intersect, since $|U|=k+c<2k$. If seven core edges cannot be pierced by two points, no point belongs to five of them: such a point together with a point in the intersection of the remaining two would pierce them. Consequently their total incidence is at most $4|U|$, which contradicts
\[
7k>4(k+c)
\]
because $c<2k/3<3k/4$.

*One anchor and six core edges.* Suppose $B,E_1,\ldots,E_6$ cannot be pierced by two points, where $E_i\in\binom Uk$. Write $P_i=U\setminus E_i$, so $|P_i|=c$. Every pair of distinct points in $U$ with at least one endpoint in $C$ must belong to at least one $P_i$: the pair already meets $B$, so otherwise it would meet every edge in the tuple. For $z\in U$ put $t(z)=\{i:z\in P_i\}$.

Every point $z\in C$ satisfies $|t(z)|\ge3$. A zero type would make $z$ itself a transversal. If $1\le|t(z)|\le2$, every other point of $U$ lies in some $P_i$ with $i\in t(z)$; $z$ itself also lies in that union. Thus at most two $c$-sets cover $U$, forcing $k+c\le2c$, contrary to $c<k$.

Every point $z\in A$ satisfies $|t(z)|\ge2$. Its type cannot be empty, since $C$ is nonempty. If $t(z)=\{i\}$, then pairing $z$ with each point of $C$ forces $C\subseteq P_i$. But $|P_i|=|C|=c$, so $P_i=C$, contradicting $z\in P_i$.

Counting incidences in the six complements now gives
\[
6c=\sum_{i=1}^6|P_i|=\sum_{z\in U}|t(z)|\ge2k+3c,
\]
which implies $c\ge2k/3$, a contradiction. Smaller subfamilies can be padded by repetitions, so the convention “at most seven” is satisfied. This completes the proof.

In particular, take $k=3m$ and $c=2m-1$. Then $\tau(\mathcal H)=2m=2k/3$. Hence the asymptotic extremal coefficient among $(7,2)$ families possessing two disjoint edges is **at least $2/3$**. The previously recorded $11/20$ is the exact value only for the more symmetric two-part type-closed class.

**Exact boundary witness.** At $k=6t,c=4t$, split $A$ into three classes of size $2t$, with types $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{5,6\}$, and split $C$ into four classes of size $t$, with types
\[
\{1,3,5\},\quad\{1,4,6\},\quad\{2,3,6\},\quad\{2,4,5\}.
\]
Let $P_i$ consist of classes whose types contain $i$. Each $P_i$ has size $4t$, so $E_i=U\setminus P_i$ has size $6t$. Every two $C$ types intersect and every $A$ type intersects every $C$ type. Thus pairs with a $C$ endpoint miss an $E_i$; pairs in $A$ miss $B$; and any point of $D$ misses all core edges, whose common intersection is empty. Therefore $B,E_1,\ldots,E_6$ is a bad tuple. The strict threshold in the proposition reflects a real obstruction, rather than a loss in its counting proof.

**Consequence for the proposed pipeline.** An attempted “anchor absorption” lemma claiming that after a minimum cover of the edges disjoint from $A$, the remainder always has transversal at most $11k/20+O(1)$ is false. In this construction the only edge disjoint from $A$ is $B$, so that auxiliary cover has size one. Deleting all edges through one chosen point of $B$ leaves a complete core with transversal at least $c$ (and exactly $c+1$ if the point lies in $D$). This tends to $2k/3$.


### 7.86 A cross-only obstruction above $3/4$


Take disjoint $k$-sets $A,B$ and a subset $A'\subset A$ of size $a$, where
\[
3k/4<a<4k/5.
\]
Let $\mathcal G=\{A\}\cup\binom{A'\cup B}{k}$. Its transversal number is $a+1$: the complete core gives the lower bound, and any $(a+1)$-set of the core containing a point of $A'$ meets the anchor as well.

Nevertheless, any five edges of $\mathcal G$ are met by a pair $x\in A',y\in B$. Indeed, a core edge $E$ misses precisely the cross pairs in the rectangle
\[
(A'\setminus E)\times(B\setminus E).
\]
The side sizes sum to $a$, so its area is at most $a^2/4$. Five such rectangles have total area at most $5a^2/4<ak=|A'\times B|$ and cannot cover all cross pairs. The anchor $A$ misses none of these pairs. This proves cross-(5,1).

The family does fail full $(7,2)$: for ranks divisible by four its complete core contains the Fano-complement seven-tuple as soon as $a\ge3k/4$. Thus tuples omitting one fixed anchor are essential even for the **$3/4$** target; the earlier cross-only barrier of $2/3$ understated the obstruction.


### 7.87 A simultaneous criticality normal form for a counterexample

The preceding improvements of local methods do not supply a general proof. The following reduction retains global information which a finite response game discards. It is a hand argument; the final structural inequality remains open.

**Lemma 7.87.** Fix integers $k,t$ with $t>1+\lceil k/2\rceil$. If a rank-at-most-$k$ $(7,2)$-family with transversal number at least $t$ exists, choose one with the fewest nonisolated vertices, and then with the fewest incidences. Denote it by $\mathcal H$, and its number of vertices by $n$. Then:

1. $\tau(\mathcal H)=t$. For each edge $E$, there is a $(t-1)$-set $T_E$ disjoint from $E$ which meets every other edge. Consequently $T_E\cup\{x\}$ is a minimum transversal for every $x\in E$.
2. Every two distinct vertices occur together in a minimum transversal.
3. Every edge satisfies $|E|\ge t-\lfloor(k+4)/5\rfloor$. For each incidence $x\in E$ with $|E|\ge2$, there are at most six other actual edges $F_1,\ldots,F_q$ with empty common intersection such that
   $$P(F_1,\ldots,F_q)\cap E=\{x\},$$
   where $P$ is the set of endpoints of two-point transversals. This $P$ itself meets every edge of $\mathcal H$.
4. The smallest possible width $q$ of such a certificate is five or six. At width five, the nonempty set
   $$C=\bigcap_{i:x\notin F_i}F_i$$
   is disjoint from $E$, has size at least $t-1$, and meets every edge avoiding $x$. At minimum width six, replacing $E$ by $E\setminus\{x\}$ gives a seven-edge family with transversal number three, every proper subfamily of which is two-pierceable.

*Proof.* Passing from uniformity to rank at most $k$ is legitimate. Pad each shorter nonempty edge by its own private vertices. Property $(7,2)$ is preserved, and any cover of the padded family gives a cover of the original family of no greater size by replacing a private vertex by a point in its original edge. The reverse transversal inequality follows because every original cover still works. Thus this change of formulation preserves the extremal problem.

Deleting an edge preserves $(7,2)$ and reduces the number of vertices or incidences. By minimality, the remaining transversal number is at most $t-1$. Restoring a nonempty edge increases it by at most one. This proves exact edge criticality and the existence of $T_E$. Such a cover cannot meet $E$, since otherwise it would cover the whole family with $t-1$ points.

Identify two vertices $u,v$ to a single vertex. Images of the original piercing pairs still pierce the image edges, so $(7,2)$ and the rank bound are preserved. The new transversal number lies between $t-1$ and $t$. It equals $t-1$ if and only if some original minimum transversal contains both $u,v$: merging that cover proves one direction; lifting a smaller cover by replacing the merged vertex with $u,v$ proves the other. If no such minimum cover existed, identification would preserve $t$ on fewer vertices, a contradiction. This proves assertion 2. Equivalently, every pair of vertices is disjoint from some maximum independent set.

For the edge-size bound, the family of edges disjoint from $E$ is six-wise intersecting: a pair piercing six such edges and $E$ must use one point in $E$, and its other point must meet all six. The usual intersection-chain argument for a $p$-wise intersecting rank-$k$ family gives a cover of size at most $\lfloor(k+p-2)/(p-1)\rfloor$. Covering that residual family and taking all of $E$ proves the claimed lower bound on $|E|$.

Delete one incidence $x\in E$, leaving $E\setminus\{x\}\ne\varnothing$. This cannot decrease the transversal number. The new family has fewer incidences or vertices, so it must fail $(7,2)$. A bad subfamily consists of the modified edge and at most six unchanged edges $F_1,\ldots,F_q$. The original tuple containing $E$ has a two-point transversal. Every such pair must touch $E$ only at $x$; otherwise it also covers the modified edge. Conversely an eligible point in $E\setminus\{x\}$ would repair the bad tuple. This proves the displayed singleton intersection. The $F_i$ have empty common intersection, since a common point together with any point of $E\setminus\{x\}$ would again repair it. Their eligible set $P$ covers the whole family: add any one edge to the at most six $F_i$ and use $(7,2)$.

The short-width conclusion follows from the more general observation proved next. If $q\le5$, put $p=6-q$. The core $C$ above is nonempty, because $x$ is eligible, and at least one witness row misses $x$, because the common intersection of all witnesses is empty. Also $C\cap E=\varnothing$: a point $y\in C\cap E$ would pair with $x$ to cover all witnesses, making $y$ a second eligible point of $E$.

Take any $p$ edges avoiding $x$. Together with $E$ and the $q$ witnesses they form at most seven edges. Every piercing pair must contain $x$; its other point belongs to $C$ and to all $p$ new edges. Their traces on $C$ are therefore $p$-wise intersecting. Partition $C$ into $p$ parts as equally as possible. Some part meets every edge avoiding $x$, since otherwise choosing one edge avoiding each part would contradict that intersection property. Hence
$$\tau(\mathcal H)\le1+\left\lceil\frac{|C|}{6-q}\right\rceil.$$
For $q\le4$ this is at most $1+\lceil k/2\rceil$, contrary to the chosen $t$. At width five it gives $|C|\ge t-1$ and the stated cover property. Finally, a minimum-width six certificate becomes a bad seven-tuple after deleting the incidence. Removing the modified edge leaves an original six-edge subfamily; removing any other edge restores two-pierceability by minimum width. Its transversal number is exactly three, since a cover of any six rows together with one point of the seventh has size at most three. $\square$

In the intended regime $t>3k/4$, the edge-size estimate is $|E|>11k/20-4/5$, so singleton edges are absent for sufficiently large $k$. Thus every incidence is governed by the normal form. The width-five and width-six alternatives must hold simultaneously across all incidences; isolated local configurations without this consistency are not counterexamples to this reduction.

The point-identification argument is an additional global reduction, not a theorem that such a counterexample is impossible. The remaining task is to reconcile its minimum covers with all of its forcing certificates and derive $4t\le3k+o(k)$. No such inequality is claimed here.

### 7.88 A ground-set reduction that would close the full proof

**Lemma 7.88 (Fano partition bound).** Every $(7,2)$-family on $n$ vertices satisfies
$$\alpha(\mathcal H)\ge4\lfloor n/7\rfloor,\qquad
\tau(\mathcal H)\le n-4\lfloor n/7\rfloor<3n/7+4.$$

*Proof.* Partition the vertices into seven classes of sizes $\lfloor n/7\rfloor$ or $\lceil n/7\rceil$, labelled by the seven points of the Fano plane. For each Fano line form the union of the four classes outside that line. If all seven unions contained an edge, choosing one contained edge from each would give a bad seven-tuple: the labels of any two proposed piercing points lie on a Fano line, whose complementary union misses both. The same reasoning works when their labels coincide. Thus one union is independent and contains at least $4\lfloor n/7\rfloor$ vertices. Taking its complement gives the transversal bound. $\square$

This isolates a sufficient *open* global bridge. If the normal form in Lemma 7.87 could be shown to satisfy
$$n\le k+t+o(k),$$
then Lemma 7.88 would give $t\le3(k+t)/7+o(k)$, and hence $t\le3k/4+o(k)$. Equivalently, the missing kernel statement is $\alpha(\mathcal H)\le k+o(k)$ for a hypothetical high-transversal counterexample after all safe vertex identifications.

That kernel bound is not asserted unconditionally. The two-part pocket, for example, has $\tau\sim11k/20$ and can have maximum independent sets much larger than $k$. Likewise, general vertex-critical hypergraphs need not have order close to rank plus transversal number. The high-transversal hypothesis and the full local property must be used. The current program treats this kernel route, the two forcing-certificate widths, and the anchored disjoint-edge tradeoff as distinct possible bridges; none has yet been completed.


### 7.89 Singleton intersections exclude uniformly persistent outside classes

**Lemma 7.89 (hand proof).** In the normal form of Lemma 7.87, every vertex is the intersection of at most six actual edges containing it. If the family is intersecting, five edges suffice. An incidence with a width-five certificate in an intersecting family needs at most four.

*Proof.* Fix an incidence $x\in E$ and a witness $F_1,\ldots,F_q$ with $q\le6$ and $P(F_1,\ldots,F_q)\cap E=\{x\}$. Put $J=\{i:x\in F_i\}$. A piercing pair containing $x$ has a partner $z$ in every row outside $J$. If another point $y$ belonged to $E\cap\bigcap_{i\in J}F_i$, the pair $y,z$ would also pierce every witness row, contradicting singleton eligibility. Here $z\notin E$, as proved for the partner core in Lemma 7.87, so the pair has distinct points. Therefore
$$E\cap\bigcap_{i\in J}F_i=\{x\}.$$
At least one row misses $x$, so $|J|\le5$. In an intersecting family at least two rows miss $x$: otherwise the unique such row would be the partner core, disjoint from $E$. Thus $|J|\le4$, or $|J|\le3$ at width five. Including $E$ proves the claims. $\square$

Consequently, suppose a nonempty class $R$ has the property that every actual edge either misses $R$ or omits at most $d$ of its points. Apply the lemma to $x\in R$. Each of its at most six isolating edges omits at most $d$ points of $R$, so
$$|R|\le6d+1.$$
The intersecting bounds are $5d+1$, or $4d+1$ at a width-five incidence. This is a constraint on **all actual edges**. It does not say that a class with identical membership in one observed tuple is small. In particular, a local defense in which every future edge contains all but $d$ points of a class of size greater than $7d$ cannot persist in the critical normal form.

### 7.90 Exact residual transversals and the outside exchange defect

**Lemma 7.90 (hand proof).** Let $\tau(\mathcal H)=t$ and let an edge $E$ have a disjoint $(t-1)$-set $B$ meeting every other edge. For $Y\subseteq B$ define
$$\mathcal H_Y=\{F\in\mathcal H:F\cap(B\setminus Y)=\varnothing\}.$$
Then $\tau(\mathcal H_Y)=|Y|+1$.

*Proof.* A smaller cover, together with $B\setminus Y$, would cover $\mathcal H$ with fewer than $t$ points. Conversely, $Y\cup\{e\}$ covers $\mathcal H_Y$ for every $e\in E$, since $E$ is its only edge disjoint from $B$. $\square$

In particular, if nonempty $X\subseteq E$ and $Y\subseteq B$ have equal size $q$, an actual edge $F$ avoids $(B\setminus Y)\cup X$. It differs from $E$, and has nonempty $B$-trace contained in $Y$. One may also forbid an external set $Z$ when $|X|+|Z|=|Y|$ and $X\ne\varnothing$. The condition excluding $E$ is necessary; with $X=\varnothing$, $E$ itself can answer the request.

If $E$ is a smallest edge, put $e=|E|$, $r=|F\cap B|$, and $h=|(E\setminus X)\setminus F|$. For an equal-size exchange request,
$$|F\setminus(E\cup B)|\ge q-r+h.$$
Indeed $|F\cap E|=e-q-h$ and $|F|\ge e$. Thus a response contained in $E\cup B$ must be exactly $(E\setminus X)\cup Y$. If every such request admits a response contained there, the family contains every $e$-subset of $E\cup B$. This conditional conclusion supplies a complete homogeneous core; no argument yet forces the required internal responses.

There is a weaker sufficient core reduction. Put $U=E\cup B$. If $L\subseteq V\setminus U$ meets every edge not contained in $U$, the family remaining after taking $L$ lies on $|U|=e+t-1$ vertices. Lemma 7.88, with $n-4\lfloor n/7\rfloor\le3n/7+24/7$, gives
$$t\le |L|+\frac{3(e+t-1)+24}{7},\qquad
t\le\frac34e+\frac74|L|+\frac{21}{4}.$$
Therefore an outside cover of size $o(k)$ for some such critical pair would prove the desired asymptotic upper bound. Existence of that cover is **open**. It is weaker than bounding the entire number of outside vertices.

### 7.91 Joint minimization gives two global exchange transversals

Fix the finite ground set $V=\bigcup\mathcal H$, with $|V|\ge2$. For a six-tuple $\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_6)$ of actual edges, repetitions allowed, let $\Pi(\mathcal F)$ be its unordered two-point transversals, using distinct points of $V$, and let $P(\mathcal F)$ be their endpoint set. Choose a tuple minimizing
$$\bigl(|P(\mathcal F)|,\ |\Pi(\mathcal F)|\bigr)$$
lexicographically over **all** six-tuples. Tuples with a common point are included; their endpoint set is $V$. This convention is important because a replacement can acquire a common point.

Write $\Pi=\Pi(\mathcal F)$ and $P=P(\mathcal F)$. For each $i$, let
$$A_i=\Pi(\mathcal F\setminus\{F_i\})\setminus\Pi,$$
where omission means omission of that indexed occurrence. Let $W_i$ be the endpoint set of $A_i$. Every pair in $A_i$ misses $F_i$, so $W_i\cap F_i=\varnothing$. Let $Q_i$ be the endpoint set of those pairs in $A_i$ having at least one endpoint outside $P$. Finally let $N(x)=\{y:\{x,y\}\in\Pi\}$.

**Lemma 7.91 (hand proof).** The following sets are transversals of the entire family:

1. $W_i\cup\{u,v\}$ for every $\{u,v\}\in\Pi$;
2. $\{x\}\cup N(x)\cup Q_i$ for every $x\in P\cap F_i$.

*Proof.* If an actual edge $G$ avoided the first set, replace $F_i$ by $G$. No pair in $A_i$ survives, while the old pair $\{u,v\}$ is lost. The new pair set is a proper subset of $\Pi$. Its endpoint set either shrinks, or stays the same while the number of pairs decreases, contradicting the chosen minimum.

If $G$ avoided the second set, the replacement loses every old pair containing $x$. Any newly admitted pair with an endpoint outside $P$ has both endpoints in $Q_i$ and cannot survive. The new endpoint set is consequently contained in $P\setminus\{x\}$, again a contradiction. These arguments include replacements having a common point because the minimization includes them. $\square$

As always, $P$ is itself a global transversal by $(7,2)$. If
$$\delta_i=\min_{\{u,v\}\in\Pi}|\{u,v\}\setminus W_i|\in\{0,1,2\},$$
the first conclusion gives $t\le |W_i|+\delta_i$.

The joint choice excludes both earlier scalar-potential examples. In Lemma 7.81 no pair is newly admitted on omitting one old row, so $W_i=\varnothing$ and the joint-minimum hypothesis would imply $t\le2$. For the twenty equal triple cells in Lemma 7.83 every original point is eligible and no degree-zero point can help cover five rows. Thus $Q_i=\varnothing$, and the second conclusion gives $t\le m+1$ from a complementary triple cell of size $m$. These deductions do not assert that every possible six-row support is excluded.

### 7.92 A conditional counting proof at the exact coefficient

For the jointly minimizing tuple above, set
$$d(v)=|\{i:v\in F_i\}|,\qquad q(v)=|\{i:v\in W_i\}|.$$
Since $W_i$ misses $F_i$, $q(v)\le6-d(v)$. Define the signed incidence deficit
$$D(\mathcal F)=\sum_{v\in V}\bigl(q(v)+2\mathbf1_{v\in P}-d(v)\bigr).$$

**Lemma 7.92 (hand proof).** Every rank-at-most-$k$ $(7,2)$-family satisfies, for its jointly minimizing tuple,
$$8t\le6k+D(\mathcal F)+\sum_{i=1}^6\delta_i\le6k+D(\mathcal F)+12.$$

*Proof.* Sum the six bounds $t\le|W_i|+\delta_i$ and twice the bound $t\le|P|$. By the definition of $D$,
$$8t-\sum_i\delta_i\le\sum_i|W_i|+2|P|
=\sum_i|F_i|+D(\mathcal F)\le6k+D(\mathcal F).$$
This is the required inequality. $\square$

In particular, suppose every noneligible vertex in $V$ has degree at least three and every eligible vertex has degree at least four. Then each summand in $D$ is nonpositive: for the former points use $q-d\le6-2d$, and for the latter use $q+2-d\le8-2d$. Hence
$$t\le3k/4+3/2.$$
More generally the same asymptotic conclusion follows if the total positive part of $D$ is $o(k)$. Positive summands can occur only at noneligible points of degree at most two or eligible points of degree at most three. Controlling these points at a global minimum is a precise **open** structural step. It is weaker than requiring a Fano support, but it has not been proved for arbitrary families.

For the six-row Fano support of Lemma 7.82, the noneligible classes have degree three and the eligible classes degree four. Each $W_i$ contains one eligible class, so $\delta_i=1$. The counting proof directly gives $t\le3k/4+3/4$, without the equal-atom-mass or quadratic pair-count computation. This conditional calculation is a new use of joint minimization, not a resolution of Problem 644.


### 7.93 A five-row neighborhood profile governing a second response

The endpoint minimum in Section 7.91 gives a constraint on every five-tuple of actual edges, including five-tuples formed after a first new response. Let $m$ be the minimum endpoint count over all six-tuples on the fixed ground set $V$.

**Lemma 7.93 (hand proof).** Let $K$ be the graph of two-point transversals of any five actual edges, let $P_5$ be its endpoint set, and let $S\subseteq P_5$ satisfy $|S|>|P_5|-m$. Then its closed neighborhood
$$N_K[S]=S\cup\{v:\text{some }s\in S\text{ has }\{s,v\}\in E(K)\}$$
is a transversal of $\mathcal H$.

*Proof.* If an actual edge $G$ avoided $N_K[S]$, no pair containing any point of $S$ could pierce the five rows together with $G$: both endpoints of such a pair would miss $G$. The six-tuple would have at most $|P_5|-|S|<m$ eligible endpoints, contradicting the definition of $m$. $\square$

Here is a relative form useful for two successive responses. Fix a minimizing six-tuple with endpoint set $P$, and take a five-tuple consisting of four selected actual rows and a new actual edge $G_1$. Put $R=P_5\setminus P$. If $c\in P\setminus G_1$, then
$$D=(G_1\cap P_5)\cup R\cup N_K(R\cap G_1)\cup\{c\}$$
is a global transversal, where $N_K$ denotes open neighborhood.

Indeed $G_1\cap P_5$ is a vertex cover of $K$. For any $r\in R\setminus G_1$, all its neighbors belong to that vertex cover. For $r\in R\cap G_1$, its neighbors are explicitly included in $D$. Thus $D$ contains $N_K[R]$. If $c\in P_5$, its neighbors also lie in $G_1\cap P_5$, since $c\notin G_1$; hence $D$ contains $N_K[R\cup\{c\}]$. That set qualifies in the lemma because $P_5\cap P$ has at most $m$ points. If instead $c\notin P_5$, then $|P_5\cap P|\le m-1$, and $R$ alone qualifies. This proves the relative claim in both cases.

Consequently, when $G_1\cap R=\varnothing$ and $P\setminus G_1\ne\varnothing$,
$$\tau(\mathcal H)\le |G_1\cap P_5|+|R|+1.$$
This forces a large old trace whenever a first response introduces only a few eligible points outside the original minimum. It does not bound $R$ for arbitrary responses; that is the remaining issue in applying it to all six-row supports. Unlike a single replacement calculation, the five-tuple here can contain the first response and only four original rows.

#### Target and the first failed shortcut

For normalized rank one, write N=x+y. Suppose a closed trace set C has an

    t = tau* = N-1-g.

**Theorem [C].** Let C be a nonempty closed admissible trace set over two parts
of capacities x,y, with rank normalized to one. Let g be its largest internal
gap (zero if there are no gaps). Suppose its continuous transversal coefficient
satisfies t=N-1-g, so a mixed free residual box is optimal. If the family has
property (7,2) and t>2/3, then N+t<=5/2.

The exact relation to finite pair extendibility is proved below. Passing from
property (7,2) at one integer scale to the continuous property requires a
separate rounding argument; that passage is not silently assumed.

The complete two-type template menu does not suffice. A small exact linear
arithmetic search gives

    x=6747/20960, y=1957/1310,
    C={0,267/2096,271/1048},
    g=275/2096, t=14349/20960>2/3,
    N+t=6551/2620>5/2.

Every pair of these three traces passes all 42 two-type exclusions. This is not
a counterexample to the target: a tuple using all three types fails (7,2).
The following hand construction explains the failure directly.

#### A three-type trimmed-Fano lemma, with explicit masses

Let a<=q<=c be three actual admissible traces. Assign the seven Fano row labels
the types a,q,q,q,q,c,c, putting the a row and the two c rows on a Fano line.
The seven complementary four-row cells form three symmetry classes:

* one cell consisting of the four q rows;
* two cells, each containing two q rows and both c rows;
* four cells, each containing the a row, two q rows, and one c row.

Put mass f in the first cell, mass b in each of the two cells, and mass d in
each of the four cells. The loads at the a,q,c rows are respectively

    4d, f+b+2d, 2b+2d,

and total mass is f+2b+4d.

In the first part choose

    d=a/4,
    b=c/2-a/4,
    f=max(0,q-c/2-a/4).

These are nonnegative, their row loads dominate a,q,c, and their total is

    A(a,q,c)=max(c+a/2, q+c/2+a/4).

In the second part choose

    d=(1-a)/4,
    b=max(0,(1+a-2c)/4),
    f=max(0,(1+a)/2-q-b).

These loads dominate 1-a,1-q,1-c. If b>0, the last displayed f is
(1+a+2c-4q)/4>=0 because q<=c<(1+a)/2. If b=0, its given maximum is used.
In the two cases the total is respectively 7/4-a/4-q-c/2 and
max(1-a,3/2-a/2-q). Thus in all cases it equals

    B(a,q,c)=max(1-a, 3/2-a/2-q, 7/4-a/4-q-c/2).

Consequently, if x>=A(a,q,c) and y>=B(a,q,c), there is a bad seven-tuple.
Indeed the masses fit in their respective parts; trim excess membership from
each individual row to obtain exactly its prescribed trace in each part.
Trimming replaces Fano-complement cells by subsets. Two such cells cannot cover
all seven row labels, so trimming preserves the obstruction. Unused capacity
lies outside every row. This construction is valid over reals, and over integer
scales after rational scaling.

For the displayed three-type candidate, take a=0, q=267/2096, c=271/1048.
Here A=c and B=31300/20960. The capacities are x=6747/20960>c and
y=31312/20960>B, so the failure is a hand-checked consequence of the formula.

#### A precise interval-covering consequence

Let C be closed with largest internal gap g, and let delta=N-7/4>0. Suppose
g<2delta. Fix a,q,h in C such that

    a<=q<=h,
    h<=x-a/2,
    q>=3/2-y-a/2.

If

    7/2-2y-a/2-2q <= h,
    2x-a/2-2q >= q,

then the three-type construction gives a bad tuple, with some high trace c in
C intersected with [q,h]. To see this, consider the partner interval

    I=[7/2-2y-a/2-2q, 2x-a/2-2q].

It has length 2delta>g and meets [q,h]. If I contains either endpoint q or h,
it already contains an actual trace in [q,h]. Otherwise it lies inside (q,h)
and cannot avoid C, because its length exceeds the largest gap. Choose c in
the intersection. The endpoint conditions imply c+a/2<=x and
3/2-a/2-q<=y; membership in I gives both remaining total-mass inequalities.
The condition 1-a<=y follows from admissibility. The lemma applies.

Equivalently, whenever a,h in C satisfy a<=h<=x-a/2, the absence of a bad tuple
forces C to miss the middle-trace interval

    [max(a,3/2-y-a/2,(7/2-2y-a/2-h)/2),
     min(h,(2x-a/2)/3)].

This is a concrete interval propagation rule, not an informal assertion that
the type set behaves convexly.

#### Reduction to four actual types

Suppose toward the density target that t>2/3 and N+t>5/2. Let l=min C and
c=max C. Mixed optimality gives

    y<=1-l+g if l>0,
    x<=c+g if c<1.

Also g<=c-l. Since N+t=2N-1-g>5/2, we have delta>g/2>=0.

The homogeneous Fano forbidden interval is

    H=[1-4y/7,4x/7].

There must be actual types on both sides. If all are above H, then l>0 and
x<7l/4. Consequently

    N+t=2(x+y)-1-g < 1+3l/2+g
        <=1+l/2+c <=5/2,

a contradiction. If all are below H, then c<1 and y<7(1-c)/4, giving

    N+t < 5/2-3c/2+g <=5/2-c/2-l <=5/2,

again a contradiction.

By compactness choose consecutive types a,b straddling H. They obey

    l<=a<b<=c,
    a<1-4y/7, b>4x/7,
    b-a<=g.

These four actual values l,a,b,c, the two endpoint cover conditions, the density
violation, and exclusion of a small number of two- and three-type constructions
already form an inconsistent QF_LRA system in discovery. No discretization of C
or assumption that it has only four elements was made.

#### The completed compact finite argument [C]

`agent_kernel_gap_core.json` records the initial 23-assertion discovery core.
The completed certificate reconstructs these conditions independently, adding
only elementary valid bounds. The substantive conditions consist of:

* nine feasibility/order/central-gap conditions;
* the two endpoint cover bounds;
* t>2/3 and N+t>5/2;
* the existing two-type functions M0,M2,M5,M6,M7,M8,M9 at (a,b), and M1 at (l,b);
* the new triple (l,a,c), and the part-reflected new triple (l,b,c).

The stronger one-versus-six span inequality is unnecessary.

To express strict inequalities using closed rational polyhedra, introduce a
common gamma>0. Each strict positive quantity is required to be at least gamma.
This is valid because a hypothetical counterexample has only finitely many
strict conditions and construction exclusions under consideration: choose one
positive excess in each exclusion and then a sufficiently small common gamma.
We can assume gamma<=1. All eight variables (x,y,l,c,a,b,g,gamma) are treated as
free in the rational linear-combination checks; every sign or upper bound used
is an explicit row.

Each no-construction assertion is a disjunction of rational linear inequalities.
The two endpoint-cover assertions are also disjunctions, with an equality as one
alternative. A finite branching tree splits these disjunctions. Every split
contains every alternative exactly once; leaves may close before all remaining
disjunctions are split, since inconsistency then already follows. There are
3,258 nodes and 2,744 leaves.

At a leaf write the selected system as Av<=b. The certificate supplies sparse
rational multipliers z_i<0. Either

    z^T A=0 and z^T b>0,

contradicting feasibility, or

    z^T A=-e_gamma^T and z^T b>=0,

forcing gamma<=0. All equalities and inequalities are checked with Python
`fractions.Fraction`. The 2,744 leaves use 18,442 nonzero multipliers in total.

The eight construction records are positive witnesses only. For each listed
capacity function M(s,t), its fixed bad parent support and coloring are checked.
At the coordinate rays and every corner ray of M, explicit nonnegative parent
masses meet all seven row demands and have total M(s,t). Between consecutive

therefore gives a realization of the asserted cost throughout that cone.
Trimming preserves the bad support. This verifies sufficiency of the eight
constructions without checking, assuming, or importing completeness of the
